text: {"answer":"The evidence mostly argues against routine daily vitamin D supplementation for healthy adults, though the picture is mixed. Large trials in vitamin D-replete adults found no effect on cancer, cardiovascular events, type 2 diabetes, bone density or falls [fbce4d7a6120#3]. The Finnish trial found no lower rates of major cardiovascular events or invasive cancer in older adults, possibly because most already had sufficient status [0dafa2c8c11c#3]. VITAL found no reduction in fracture risk among generally healthy midlife and older adults not selected for deficiency [d8b33533d51c#3]. A meta-analysis found no reduction in all-cause mortality, though cancer death fell by 16% [81282aae0b32#2]. The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against supplementation for fracture prevention in healthy postmenopausal women [9c98e4515e3d#0]. On the other side, the Endocrine Society suggests empiric supplementation for adults aged 75 and older and for high-risk prediabetes, citing potential mortality and diabetes-progression benefits [8279771cfc3d#4]. Some evidence suggests deficient individuals or prediabetic patients may benefit from long-term supplementation [58487bc44db2#1]. Overall, routine daily use is not clearly supported for generally healthy adults, while targeted use in deficiency or specific groups remains debated.","confidence":62,"one_line":"Routine daily vitamin D for healthy adults lacks benefit in major trials; targeted use in older or high-risk adults remains debated."}
